newsitem.title: CHINA: ASIA WEEK AHEAD - Asian stocks seen volatile.
newsitem.headline: ASIA WEEK AHEAD - Asian stocks seen volatile.

text.p: Asian shares face a volatile trading week, with Hong Kong poised for further gains, some smaller markets poised for technical recovery but the rest of the region on tenterhooks about recent currency turmoil.
On Friday, the Philippine Central Bank halted a defence of the peso's peg to the U.S. dollar while Indonesia further widened the trading band for the rupiah.
Speculators and hedge funds remain active in the region.
Attention has now focused on the Malaysian ringgit as a wave of speculation that started with Thailand's July 2 float and effective devaluation of the baht continued to roll throughout Asia.

Although stock markets in Bangkok and Manila welcomed the increased currency flexibility, the regional mood remains uncertain while investors wait to see the effects of the new currency regimes filter through a troubled economic landscape.

Sentiment remained weak among foreign investors, and regional traders reported that net outflows continued unabated last week. Little improvement is forecast next week, although Hong Kong is expected to continue roaring ahead on post-handover optimism. The territory returned to Chinese control on July 1.

TOKYO - The Tokyo stock market's key index should be trapped in a narrow range this week, caught between two forces -- buying of financially healthy blue-chip issues, especially high techs, and the sell-off of shares in firms with financial problems, brokers said.
On Friday, the 225-share Nikkei average finished at 19,875.49, down 92.51 points from the close a week earlier.

Market strategists expect the Nikkei 225 index to trade narrowly for the time being, as growing concerns about some Japanese companies, including contractors, retailers and brokers, weighed on the market.
But at the same time, such movements would prompt investors actively to seek promising issues.

"I expect the polarisation trend to continue next week, as high-techs will remain upbeat but issues with credit risks will decline," said Hiroyuki Nakai, chief investment strategist at Nikko Securities Co Ltd. - - - - HONG KONG - Share prices are expected to continue gaining on follow-through buying after Friday's fresh record closing high, brokers said.

Active futures buying lifted the Hang Seng index of blue chips stocks 386.06 points to close at 15,225.29 on Friday, but the longer term direction remained uncertain as the market waited for government measures to rein in property prices.

"It is hard to judge whether the market is going to consolidate more around 15,300 or whether there is a breakout," said Howard Gorges at South China Brokerage. The Hang Seng gained 402.32 points, or 2.71 percent, to close the week at 15,225.29 on Friday.

TAIPEI - Taiwan share prices are expected to follow their recent bull runs and test new highs next week, but brokers said investors would become cautious as the index moved towards heavy 9,600-point resistance.

The central bank's repeated issuances of negotiable certificates of deposit, widely seen as an attempt to keep a lid on the loose liquidity that many experts said was fuelling the stock rally, would add caution, brokers said.
"The central bank's persistent moves to tighten liquidity will soon show its effect," said Taiwan Securities Investment's analyst Joe Chiou.
"The index will have difficulty to breach its key 9,600-point resistance without the support of loose funds," Chiou said.
Bellwether electronics and the recovering construction sector will be the market's main focus next week, brokers said.
Brokers said the Philippine peso's plunge had no impact on Taiwan's market.
On Saturday, the index finished 106.45 points or 1.13 percent higher at 9,501.08, up 2.62 percent from 9,258.63 a week earlier.
A 9,300-9,600 range was seen for next week.
No major economic indicators were scheduled to be announced next week.
BANGKOK - Thai stocks, which fell on profit-taking this week, are expected to advance next week on more buying by foreigners of large capitalised stocks, brokers said.
The Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET) index retreated 4.34 percent in the week to 628.55 points on Friday from a week ago. It fell 3.20 percent from Thursday.

"The market is expected to be a bit volatile next week but the index is likely to rise on buying by foreigners. Liquidity is still high due to foreign capital inflows into the country earlier this week," said Thanawat Patchimkul of Seamico Securities.

Brokers said foreign sentiment would improve with investors exploiting cheaper baht after the currency fell on Friday to a new record low of 30.03 to the U.S. dollar, weakening on the effective devaluation of the Philippine peso, dealers said.
JAKARTA - Jakarta stocks are seen mixed after last week's consolidation that hit selected blue chips particularly hard, brokers said.
A technical rebound was likely as investors picked up blue chip bargains such as Telkom and Semen Gresik.

Friday's widening of the trading band for the rupiah would also lend positive momentum to the stock market next week. The currency strengthened after central bank widened the band to 12 percent from eight percent.
On Friday, the Jakarta composite index closed at 723.42 points, against last week's close of 736.60 points. The index was off 13.18 points, or 1.80 percent, on the week.
KUALA LUMPUR - Malaysian shares were expected to remain volatile next week as southeast Asian currency turmoil and heavy shorting by foreign investors influenced the market, analysts said.
"It will still be very volatile, but I think it will not be as volatile as this week," said Ang Kok Heng, general manager at TA Asset Management.
The Composite Index of 100 large-capitalised stocks closed the week 55.71 points or 5.19 percent lower on the week.
"Any break below 1,000 (on the Composite Index) will be short-lived, but I don't see it going above 1,050," said Simon Maughan, head of research at W.I. Carr in Kuala Lumpur
SINGAPORE - Share prices will be dogged this week by worries over the region's currencies woes with investors basically shrugging off the budget speech by Finance Minister Richard Hu, brokers said.
"I think it may be a variable week, but regional concern over currencies will be more dominant in the Singapore market than the budget," a broker said.

Speculation that the Malaysian ringgit will be targeted next by speculators who forced the Thai and Philippine central banks to devalue the baht and the peso, respectively, will dominate early trading this week.
One broker said some investors may decide that some issues may be ripe for bargain-hunting this week.
"Malaysian OTC (over-the-counter) shares look firmer. It has reached the point where some are beginning to think that it's now a good opportunity to buy," he said.
The 30-share Straits Times Industrials Index (STII) finished on Friday 1.2 points down on the day at 1,967.14 compared with the previous Friday's close of 1,985.94 points.
SEOUL - Seoul stocks are expected to fall next week with blue chips consolidating further, brokers said.
"With no favourable news, the market will fall further," said Koh Soon-sik at LG Securities. "But I don't expect any sharp declines on the index."

Brokers said investors were tending to shun blue chips as there were no signs of an economic turnaround in sight. They forecast the index would move in a boxed range between 750 and 770. The composite stock index closed at 767.27, down 11.97 points or 1.54 percent from last Saturday's 779.24.

SYDNEY - Australian shares are seen entering a sorting out period with yield stocks, such as banks and insurers attracting attention, while high price-earnings (P/E) shares may come under pressure as investors look to signs of growth prospects.
The All Ordinaries index closed at 2,699.1, up 0.17 percent on Friday but down 1.25 percent on the week, with most of the week's fall due to a plunge in gold shares after bullion prices dropped.

"I think you are going to see yield stocks continue to find support, but I think you might see high P/E stocks come off as people want more evidence of growth," said Stuart Smith, dealer at stockbroker Henderson Charlton Jones.
Next week is a quiet one for corporate events, with industrial group CSR Ltd holding its annual meeting on Monday
WELLINGTON - The New Zealand share market was in fine shape to climb higher after taking a breather last week following its rise to a record high the previous week.
However, late on Friday, Reserve Bank Governor Don Brash said monetary conditions were too loose and any upward rise in interest rates could dampen the positive sentiment.
"Obviously, the Reserve Bank is signalling slightly tighter conditions are more desirable, so I think we'll get more of a consolidation than we've had," said Craig Robins at County Natwest.

Consumer Price Index data on Tuesday is likely to be the key for interest rates with the potential for a fresh rally in rates and equities if inflation in the quarter is flat. Economists forecast a 0.3 percent rise.
The barometer top 40 index closed 10 points lower for the week at 2517.
BOMBAY - Indian shares are expected to resume their rally next week after a correction broke a six-week winning streak, dealers said.

The 30-share Bombay Stock Exchange index hit a new 33-month high of 4,448.06 on Thursday before ending the week with a modest loss of 1.84 points at 4,321.98 -- closing in negative territory for the first time since the week ended May 23.

Analysts said that expectations of better corporate performances in the second half of 1997/98 (April-March), falling interest rates and reports of a pick-up in industrial production to fuel the market.
NatWest Markets analyst Anindya Chatterjee said economic data reflected improved business activity and the emergence of trends that would stimulate business sentiment.
DHAKA - A bearish trend in the Bangladesh stock market is likely to continue in the week starting on Sunday because of a cash crunch and changes at the local regulator, brokers said.

"The market is expected to maintain its downward trend next week for pressure from banks on investors for repayment of loans," one broker said. "Moreover, investors would be cautious following reported resignation of SEC chief Harunur Rashid."
The Dhaka Stock Exchange (DSE) benchmark index lost 50.33 points at 1,048.02 in the week to Thursday.
